title: Honour
note: He begins the qualities of the well-born with honour: never falling below your standing, and not staying alive when god brings you down. It comes first because it keeps their birth upright.

couplets.plain: Even things you can’t do without, give them up if they would lower you.
couplets.pm: Even if leaving them undone would cost you your life, give up acts that lower your birth. He rejects the rule of the northern books that you may do something shameful to survive when death is near. Weigh the body, which doesn’t last, against honour, which does, and don’t do them.

links.quote: give them up if they would lower you
links.reason: Says to drop whatever would lower you, even what you can’t do without.

couplets.plain: Those who want glory along with great strength of character won’t do anything unworthy, even for glory.
couplets.pm: Those who want fame and want to keep their honour won’t do anything shameful and unfit for their birth, even where it would bring fame. Honour is called great strength because it stands firm everywhere. They won’t do it even for lasting fame.

links.quote: won’t do anything unworthy, even for glory

couplets.plain: In plenty, bow low. When your means shrink, stand tall.
couplets.pm: When the well-born have great wealth, they should be humble before everyone. When they fall into want, they should not bow, and should stay at their old height. Wealth raises you, so you must lower yourself. Hardship lowers you, so you must rise.

links.reason: Asks for bending low at exactly the moment you have the most.

links.quote: When your means shrink, stand tall
links.reason: When your means shrink, that is the time to stand straightest.
A plain instruction to anyone riding high: plenty is the time to bow.

couplets.plain: People who fall from their standing are like hair fallen from the head.
couplets.pm: When the well-born leave their high standing and sink from it, they are like hair dropped from the head. Hair is cared for while it stays on the head and despised once it falls, and so are they.

links.quote: like hair fallen from the head
links.reason: Shows the price of losing your standing: to be like hair that has dropped from the head.

couplets.plain: People as high as a hill will still fall if they do something low, even a thing the size of a crab’s-eye seed.
couplets.pm: Even those raised as high as a hill by their birth will sink if they do anything that lowers them, even an act the size of a crab’s-eye seed. The acts that lower you are the shameful ones.

links.quote: will still fall if they do something low
links.reason: A lapse no bigger than a crab’s-eye seed is enough to bring such a person down.
Measures a person’s stature as a hill, then sets a tiny seed against it.

couplets.plain: It brings no fame and it won’t take you to the land of the gods. So why follow behind those who despise you?
couplets.pm: Giving up your honour and standing behind those who slight you brings no fame in this world and doesn’t lead to the world of the gods. What then does it do for you? It has neither reward and destroys your honour for nothing.

links.quote: why follow behind those who despise you?
links.reason: Asks what trailing after those who despise you could ever gain, since it brings neither fame nor the land of the gods.

links.quote: why follow behind those who despise you?

couplets.plain: Better to be called ruined there and then than to live by trailing after those who spurn you.
couplets.pm: It would be better for a man to be said to have died, not having done it, than to stay alive on what he gets by following those who slight him. This answers those who say that even without fame or heaven, you at least get wealth and stay alive.
couplets.note: கெட்டான் can mean ruined or dead. He takes it as dead.
couplets.sensitive: prefers death to living under scorn

links.quote: to live by trailing after those who spurn you

couplets.plain: When your great dignity is being destroyed, is a life of tending your flesh any medicine?
couplets.pm: When honour, the strength of high birth, is being destroyed, will a life that guards a useless body instead of dying be a medicine against death? He says “flesh” because the bare body left without honour is despised, and “medicine?” because you will die anyway.
couplets.sensitive: scorns staying alive at the cost of honour

links.quote: is a life of tending your flesh any medicine?
links.reason: Mocks saving your flesh at the cost of your dignity by asking whether that is any medicine.

couplets.plain: Like the yak that won’t live if it loses its hair, there are those who give up their life when honour demands it.
couplets.pm: They are like the yak that won’t stay alive if even one hair of its coat is lost. When it comes to the point where honour can only be had by losing life, they can’t bear it and die. Life and honour can’t both stay, so they give up life, which goes anyway, for honour, which lasts. The simile shows this is their nature.
couplets.sensitive: presents ending one's life as the answer to lost honour

links.quote: Like the yak that won’t live if it loses its hair
links.reason: Likens those who cannot bear lost honour to the yak that won’t live without its hair.

couplets.plain: The world bows down and praises the radiance of those whose honour won’t let them live on in disgrace.
couplets.pm: When disgrace came to those with honour, they did not bear it and live, but gave up life. The world bows down and praises their fame for ever. Heaven need not be mentioned, because those whose fame poets sing reach it anyway.

links.quote: The world bows down and praises the radiance
